common_name: Candle Fire Okra (AAS-Winning Red Round-Podded Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; soak seed overnight to speed germination. Candle Fire is a red, round-podded okra bred to stay tender even at a larger pod size, giving a wider harvest window than most okra before pods turn woody.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost into warm soil in full sun; thin to 18-24 inches apart. Candle Fire is an AAS-winning okra selected for round (not sharply ribbed), deep-red pods that resist the rapid fiber buildup common in older red okra varieties, so pods stay tender for harvest over a longer size range and a more forgiving picking schedule — useful in the Gulf South's fast summer growth, when okra can go from tender to woody within a day or two. The tall, upright plants are heavy producers with attractive maroon-tinted foliage and pale yellow, red-throated flowers that make the whole plant a good-looking addition to the summer vegetable garden. Like other red okra, the color is water-soluble and fades during cooking unless pods are quickly grilled, roasted, or fried rather than boiled. Harvest every day or two once pods start forming to keep the plant productive.
sources: All-America Selections — Candle Fire Okra winner announcement

common_name: Super Hero Spry Marigold (AAS-Winning Bicolor French Marigold)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Super Hero Spry is a compact, uniform French marigold bred to flower heavily without deadheading.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost, or transplant started seedlings, into well-drained soil in full sun. Super Hero Spry is an AAS-winning French marigold in a compact, uniform, well-branched habit, producing masses of bicolor red-and-gold double flowers held above the foliage rather than hidden within it. Bred for a strong self-cleaning habit, it keeps blooming heavily through the heat of summer without the regular deadheading older marigold varieties need to stay tidy and productive. Its dense, even mounding shape and reliable bloom make it a dependable choice for bedding lines, edging, and containers in hot Gulf South summers. Marigolds tolerate poor, lean soil and are best grown without heavy fertilizer, which pushes foliage at the expense of flowers; water at the base to help avoid the powdery mildew and botrytis that can affect dense marigold plantings in humid weather.

common_name: Kelos Fire Red Celosia (Heat-Tolerant Plumed Celosia)
scientific_name: Celosia argentea var. plumosa 'Kelos Fire Red'

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Kelos Fire Red is a compact, uniform plumed celosia in the Kelos landscape series, bred for weather resistance and season-long color in bedding lines.

directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Kelos Fire Red is a compact, uniform, plumed (feathery) celosia bred as a weather-resistant landscape bedding plant, producing dense, upright, velvety deep-red flame-shaped plumes held well above tidy, even foliage from early summer through frost. It was bred specifically to tolerate the heat, humidity, and heavy summer rain that cause older plumed celosia strains to flop, discolor, or rot, making it a dependable performer for Gulf South summer beds and containers where many other bedding annuals struggle. Deadhead spent plumes to extend bloom, though the Kelos series is bred to keep flowering vigorously with minimal maintenance. Plants tolerate heat and some drought once established but bloom best with consistent moisture and a light monthly feeding.
sources: Benary — Celosia Kelos series breeding documentation
